title: A squid in Hawaii hides its shadow with a lamp full of glowing bacteria

cover.alt: A tiny Hawaiian bobtail squid with large golden eyes sits on the floor of a tank, facing the camera.

body: The Hawaiian bobtail squid, whose body grows to only about 3 cm, carries a light organ packed with the glowing bacterium *Aliivibrio fischeri*. The bacteria's glow matches the light falling on the squid's back, so a predator looking up from below sees no silhouette. In return the squid feeds them sugars and amino acids. Every morning at dawn it vents up to 95% of the bacteria, possibly to save energy while it rests hidden through the day.

slides.alt: A small bobtail squid with golden eyes sits on the floor of a lab tank, then another shot shows a squid sinking into pale sand as grains settle over its back.
slides.caption: Hawaiian bobtail squid filmed by NASA in May 2021: one rests in a lab tank, then one works itself down into the sand.
slides.credit: NASA/Cory S Huston · Public domain · excerpt

slides.heading: How a squid gets its lamp

steps.label: It hatches with no bacteria at all
Mucus traps bacteria from the seawater
They fill its light organ within 10–12 hours
Their glow hides its shadow from below

slides.heading: Each dawn the squid flushes out up to 95 of every 100 of its bacteria
slides.note: Why is not fully understood; saving energy during the day is one explanation

slides.heading: Squid in orbit
slides.text: In June 2021 newly hatched bobtail squid flew to the International Space Station on the SpaceX CRS-22 cargo mission. The question: can an animal still take up its partner bacteria in near-weightlessness? NASA filmed the squid in the clip a couple of weeks before that launch.

slides.question: Why does it help the squid to glow from underneath?
slides.explanation: The glow matches the light coming down from above, so a predator looking up sees no dark shadow. This trick is called counter-illumination.
